title: 10 Questions to Ask Before Choosing a Biometric Orchestration Platform
summary: Evaluating biometric orchestration? Explore 10 questions identity, fraud, and security leaders should ask when choosing an orchestration platform.
body_markdown:
Organizations have more identity technology at their disposal than ever before.


Facial recognition,[liveness detection](https://www.aware.com/blog-liveness-detection-explained/) , document verification, device intelligence, authentication, and other capabilities can each play an important role in establishing trust. But as these technologies multiply, the challenge is shifting from simply selecting the right individual tools to determining how they should work together.


That is one reason[biometric orchestration](https://www.aware.com/blog-biometric-orchestration-intelligence-layer/) is gaining attention.


Biometric orchestration can give organizations greater control over which technologies are used, when they are used, how identity workflows are configured, and how different signals contribute to an outcome. But as the category develops, leaders need to look beyond whether a platform simply connects to multiple vendors.


The more important question is: How much control does the orchestration layer actually give you?


## Look Beyond the Number of Integrations


A platform may support several biometric technologies or vendors, but connectivity alone does not necessarily equal orchestration. Organizations should consider whether they can preserve the technology investments they already have, introduce new providers as the market evolves, and make changes without rebuilding entire identity journeys.


That distinction matters because biometric technology continues to advance. New algorithms emerge. Existing providers improve. Fraud defenses evolve. The technology that is best suited to a particular problem today may not be the best choice several years (or several threat cycles) from now.


> An orchestration strategy should therefore create optionality, not simply move vendor lock-in one layer higher.


## Ask Whether Workflows Can actually Change


Identity interactions do not all carry the same level of risk. A returning customer accessing an account may require a very different level of assurance than someone recovering an account, enrolling a new device, or authorizing a high-value transaction. Yet many identity environments still rely on workflows that are difficult to modify once they are deployed.


When evaluating orchestration, leaders should consider how easily workflows can respond to changing risk, customer behavior, business requirements, and new technologies.


Can a new verification step be introduced without a major development project? Can policies change according to the transaction? Can different biometric, identity, fraud, or risk signals influence what happens next? The goal should not be to build one perfect identity workflow. It should be to build an environment where workflows can continue to evolve.


## Understand Who Controls the Decision


Orchestration also raises an important governance question: Who ultimately determines how identity decisions are made?


Some environments provide orchestration only within a closed ecosystem. Others give enterprises greater freedom to choose providers, define policies, adjust thresholds, and determine how multiple signals contribute to an outcome. For identity, fraud, and risk leaders, that level of control can be significant. Connecting multiple technologies is useful. Being able to determine how those technologies work together, and change that logic as conditions evolve, is what turns connectivity into a broader identity strategy.


## Make Testing Part of the Operating Model


There is another question organizations should consider: how difficult is it to determine whether a different technology could perform better?


Biometric testing can be time-consuming. Comparing providers may require new integrations, environments, configurations, datasets, and analysis. As a result, organizations can end up evaluating a technology during procurement and then leaving it largely unchanged—not necessarily because it remains the best available option, but because testing alternatives is difficult.


A strong orchestration environment can help make evaluation more practical. For example, the ability to evaluate technologies in parallel, benchmark providers under comparable conditions, or introduce alternatives without rebuilding a workflow can make continuous optimization easier to operationalize. Testing should not always have to be a new project. Increasingly, it should be a capability.


## Consider How Quickly the Environment Can Adapt


This becomes even more important as fraud evolves. Deepfakes, injection attacks, synthetic media, and other emerging techniques are changing faster than many organizations can change their identity infrastructure. No single control (or provider) is likely to remain the strongest answer to every threat indefinitely.


Organizations therefore need flexibility not just for procurement purposes, but for fraud defense. The ability to introduce a new technology, layer additional controls, modify policies, or change how signals are used can shorten the distance between recognizing a weakness and responding to it. In fraud prevention, that time matters. Operating with a suboptimal control for another month, quarter, or year can mean unnecessary exposure while attackers continue to adapt.


## 10 Questions Worth Asking


Before selecting a biometric orchestration platform, identity and risk leaders should be able to answer:


1. **Can we integrate multiple biometric vendors, algorithms, and technologies?**
2. **Can we preserve and build upon technologies we already use?**
3. **Can we add or replace providers without rebuilding entire identity workflows?**
4. **Can workflows be configured and changed without extensive development?**
5. **Can policies and decision logic adapt as risk changes?**
6. **Can biometric, identity, fraud, and other signals contribute to the same outcome?**
7. **Can algorithms or providers be evaluated or executed in parallel?**
8. **Can we measure and compare vendor and algorithm performance?**
9. **Can the environment adapt as fraud techniques and business requirements change?**
10. **Can the architecture scale across additional applications, channels, users, and identity journeys?**


There will not necessarily be one correct architecture or approach to biometric orchestration. But the answers to these questions can reveal whether a platform is simply providing another way to integrate technology, or actually gives the organization meaningful control over its biometric strategy.


## Moving from Biometric Tools to Biometric Strategy


Biometric orchestration represents a broader shift in how organizations can think about identity infrastructure. The objective is not to accumulate more technologies. It is to create an environment where organizations can choose the right capabilities, apply them intelligently, measure how they perform, and change the strategy when circumstances demand it.


For leaders evaluating this emerging category, that means looking beyond today’s requirements. The more important question may be whether the architecture gives you the freedom to respond to whatever comes next.
